page: Vultr voc-m-32c-256gb-1600s-amd is an Optimized Cloud Compute instance engineered for memory-intensive and multi-threaded workloads. The server runs on a 2.0 GHz AMD EPYC processor based on the x86_64 architecture, providing 32 dedicated vCPUs across 16 physical cores with simultaneous multithreading enabled. The CPU cache architecture comprises 32 KB L1 data cache, 0.5 MB L2 cache, and 32 MB L3 cache, complemented by hardware instruction extensions including AVX, AES, SHA-NI, and BMI2.

Resource allocation includes 256.0 GB of system memory, establishing a generous 8.0 GB per vCPU ratio. Local storage is directly integrated into the instance, featuring a 1600 GB NVMe SSD. No dedicated graphics processors are bundled with this configuration. For network connectivity, the server includes one complimentary public IPv4 address.

Benchmark results demonstrate strong parallel compute execution, with stress-ng multi-core testing placing in the top 25 percent at 99,821.78, accompanied by top-tier single-core stress-ng performance. Geekbench multi-core testing achieved a strong score of 16,174.0, supported by elevated marks in code compilation with Clang (41,962.0) and ray tracing (52,832.0). Memory throughput remains in the average tier, measuring 138.44 GB/sec for uncached read blocks and 65.88 GB/sec for uncached writes. Single-threaded gzip compression scored in the bottom 25 percent at 23.36 GB/sec.

Given its high memory density and dedicated core profile, the instance offers strong resource efficiency for infrastructure demanding consistent CPU availability alongside large working sets. However, the lack of AVX-512 extensions and average memory bandwidth can constrain certain vector computation pipelines. The instance is well matched for large in-memory caching systems, transactional databases, Clang-based CI/CD builds, and extract-transform-load data processing.

This hardware allocation delivers a balance of dedicated compute cycles, sizable local NVMe capacity, and dense RAM, making it practical for in-memory databases, continuous integration build clusters, and transactional data processing environments.
